notes: \cpara{Opens with Orwell's time, when totalitarianism spread from country to country, a time the reader is said to be too young to remember. The professors who ``hailed the Soviet Union's purges as progress'' recall the essay's ``comfortable English professor defending Russian totalitarianism.''}
\cpara{Credits Orwell with seeing that human evil and muddled thinking go together, and introduces the essay's passage on political language.}
\clogic{Orwell's own claim is causal and weaker: ``the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts.''}
\cpara{Orwell on political language as ``the defence of the indefensible,'' carried out by euphemism. The quotation matches the essay.}
\cpara{Orwell's reason for plain English: it makes one's own stupid remarks obvious.}
\cpara{Names this the heart of \textsc{Overcoming Bias}, the blog where the post first appeared.}
\cpara{Argues that evil must keep people's revulsion latent, and so sets out to muddle thinking. The examples are ``the planned famines of Stalin and Mao.''}

\cfact{``Planned,'' and in the next sentence ``deliberate human intent to inflict pain and death,'' go beyond the record as it is usually summarized. Wikipedia's article on the Soviet famine of 1930--1933 gives its cause as ``Disputed; theories range from deliberate engineering to economic mismanagement.'' For the Chinese famine of 1959--1961, the causes it lists include the Great Leap Forward, ``Extreme state requisitioning of grain'' and ``systemic misinformation,'' such as inflated harvest reports; a plan to starve people is not among them. ``Tens of millions'' is within the estimates.}
\clogic{Orwell's claim, quoted above, was about political language ``In our time.'' The post makes it a law of all evil, ``wherever it exists,'' and adds no evidence for the wider claim.}
\cpara{Turns to \textsc{1984}, whose villains falsify records and photographs, and to the scene in which O'Brien tortures Winston over two plus two.}
\cpara{The torture scene from \textsc{1984}. The quotation matches the novel's text.}
\cpara{Turns on the economist Tyler Cowen, with rhetorical questions about the importance of the mind.}

\cfact{Cowen's post does not say that overcoming bias is unimportant. It questions ``a strong preference for overcoming bias, relative to other ends,'' on the ground that ``Biased estimators are one problem but not the only problem.''}
\cpara{Quotes one sentence of Cowen's and offers, with ``I hope,'' a guess at why Cowen wrote it.}

\cfact{The sentence goes on: ``especially if embedded in a broader discovery process with checks and balances.'' Cowen's point was that a blog pushing one research method ``as far as it can go'' is useful inside a larger process.}

\clogic{Cowen's ``bias'' is partly the statistician's word, as the comparison with ``biased estimators'' shows, and for the blog it means a single-minded method. Cowen's post says nothing about scope insensitivity. The question answers a view the post does not show Cowen holding.}
\cpara{Likens Cowen's view to one Orwell rejected.}

\clogic{The likeness is asserted. Chase, as Orwell reports, came ``near to claiming that all abstract words are meaningless.'' Cowen drew distinctions, between bias and ``insufficient data, lazy researchers, inefficient estimators.'' Neither is quoted saying that to admit a distinction is ``youthful naiveté''; the phrase is the post's.}

\cpara{States why the post brings in evil: overcoming bias may not look ``exciting enough'' without ``some clear evil to oppose.'' The paragraph then supplies one, and imagines the blog's readers sent to labor camps.}
\cpara{Ends with two claims about all of human history, given without evidence, and a call to arms.}

\clogic{The image sits uneasily with the author's earlier warnings, in the same sequence of the book. ``Politics Is the Mind-Killer'' (February 2007): ``Politics is an extension of war by other means. Arguments are soldiers.'' ``Are Your Enemies Innately Evil?'' (June 2007): ``Debate is war; arguments are soldiers.'' Here the enemy is ``ourselves,'' not a party, but the paragraph before has given the truth ``enemies,'' and the post has set a named critic beside Orwell's opponents.}
